clue.text: Not allowed to, carrying sailor over

indicators.note: a thing carrying something holds it inside, so the first word wraps the rest

parts.note: taken as written; it becomes the outer shell
AB, able seaman, is the usual crossword sailor
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Someone is forbidden to do something, even while giving a seaman a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not allowed to' reads as one phrase, but 'to' belongs to the wordplay and splits around the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Something taboo is forbidden by custom or social prohibition.

clue.text: Gathers, before socials, in more than one place selling confectionery

definitions.text: more than one place selling confectionery

parts.note: a tuck is a fold sewn in cloth, so gathers fabric
a hop is an informal dance or social gathering

explanation.surface: Fabric gathers made before parties in several sweet shops, a jumble of a scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' simply orders the two pieces. A tuck shop is a British school snack shop; tuck is schoolboy slang for sweets and food.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuck shops are small shops, typically at British schools, that sell sweets and snacks; the plural answer matches 'more than one'.

clue.text: Film young child? No, not visible

indicators.note: what is not visible has vanished, so these letters drop out of the word

parts.note: Italian for a baby or small child, used in English too
taken as written: the letters to be removed

explanation.surface: A query whether a film features a small child, answered that none can be seen.
explanation.walkthrough: BAMBINO loses its NO to leave the Disney film BAMBI.
explanation.definitionFit: Bambi is the 1942 Disney animated film about a young deer.

clue.text: Novel ruled out — unfair, poor marks having been received

indicators.note: something poor is in bad shape, so these words are knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, part of the fodder
taken as written, part of the fodder
M is the abbreviation for mark, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A student complains a piece of work was rejected unfairly once poor marks came back.
explanation.walkthrough: The M from 'marks' is taken in among the fodder before the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Our Mutual Friend is the last completed novel by Charles Dickens, published 1864-65.

clue.text: Lady's blouse — Georgia's blue one

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia
blue jokes are smutty or ribald
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A description of a woman's top: Georgia's blue one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blue' looks like a colour but means risqué.
explanation.definitionFit: A Garibaldi was a loose red Victorian women's blouse modelled on the shirts of Garibaldi's soldiers.

clue.text: Frown from stern master

parts.note: grim means severe or forbidding
an ace is an expert, a master of a skill

explanation.surface: A schoolboy receiving a frown from a strict teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'master' looks like a schoolmaster but means an expert.
explanation.definitionFit: A grimace is a twisted facial expression of displeasure, close to a scowl.

clue.text: One may crow, duck being in list

indicators.note: one thing being in another sits inside it, so the zero goes within the list word

parts.note: a roster is a list of names or duties
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so the letter that looks like zero

explanation.surface: Someone might boast after being dropped from the team sheet for scoring nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a score of zero; 'crow' suggests boasting but means the cock's call.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooster is a male chicken, the bird that crows at dawn.

clue.text: What one must make do with if most of bananas are rotten?

definitions.text: What one must make do with if most of bananas are rotten?

parts.words: What one must make do with if most of bananas are rotten?
parts.note: surface: a shopper picking through fruit that has mostly gone off; setter's reading: the idiom for the least poor choice among poor options, with bananas literally growing in bunches

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is taken literally: bananas come in bunches, so if most are rotten you pick the soundest one.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means the least unsatisfactory option among a group that is all poor.

clue.text: City in Crete lies devastated

indicators.note: something devastated is wrecked, so these letters are scattered and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written: nine letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A news line: a city on the island of Crete lies in ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City in Crete' suggests a Cretan town, but the city is in England.
explanation.definitionFit: Leicester is a city in the East Midlands of England.

clue.text: That is part of bride's trousseau

indicators.note: only a part of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the run starts after the B of the first word and ends at the T of the second

explanation.surface: Describing an item that belongs to a bride's collection of clothes for the marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' looks like 'this item is', but it is the definition: the Latin phrase abbreviated i.e.
explanation.definitionFit: Id est is Latin meaning that is, used to restate or clarify.

clue.text: Racehorse I'm on in training, whatever the weather

indicators.note: something in training is being worked on and shaped, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the fodder

explanation.surface: A jockey says the racehorse they ride is in training in all conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in training' looks like one phrase, but 'in' is the last word of the fodder and 'training' alone signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means regardless of conditions, literally whatever the weather does.

clue.text: Salt in tum sickened? Here's a tonic

indicators.note: something sickened is upset, so these letters are churned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the fodder

explanation.surface: Too much salt has upset your stomach, so take this remedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonic is a drink or medicine that invigorates, as a stimulant does.

clue.text: Open to view? About time

parts.note: over means about, as in talking over a matter
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Asking whether something is on show, and answering that it is nearly time.
explanation.definitionFit: Overt means done openly, not concealed, visible to all.

clue.text: Old boy's solution, not easily understood

parts.note: OB is old boy, a former pupil, plus the possessive S
a cure is a solution to a problem or illness

explanation.surface: A former pupil's answer to a problem turns out to be hard to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: An old boy is a British term for a former pupil of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: Obscure means unclear or hard to grasp in meaning.

clue.text: Igloo shown, destroyed by river

indicators.note: a destroyed thing is broken up, so these letters are rebuilt in another order

parts.note: the five letters of the word reshuffled
the Ouse is a common crossword river, in Yorkshire and elsewhere in England

explanation.surface: An igloo was put on display and then washed away by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ouse is the name of several English rivers.
explanation.definitionFit: An igloo is an Inuit dome-shaped shelter built from blocks of snow.

clue.text: Responded concerning new cadet

indicators.note: making something new remakes it, so the following word's letters are rearranged

parts.note: re means concerning, as in business letters
the five letters reordered

explanation.surface: Someone replied about a recently arrived trainee officer.
explanation.definitionFit: To react is to respond to a stimulus or event.

clue.text: Sculptor on a broadcast in celebration

indicators.note: placed in something means put inside it, so the first words go within the party word

parts.note: a do is an informal British word for a party
taken as written
taken as written
to broadcast news is to tell it widely

explanation.surface: A sculptor appears on a television programme at a celebratory event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' suggests radio or television, but here it is the verb meaning spread the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Donatello was the Florentine Renaissance sculptor of the bronze David.

clue.text: One who has wrecked aerodynamic device

definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who spoils or ruins things
second meaning: a flap or fin on a car or aircraft wing that disrupts airflow

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a crash investigator; the two halves are unrelated meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a person who ruins things and a device that spoils airflow to reduce lift.

clue.text: Lamb, for example, reportedly studied answer

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: past tense of read is said like this colour, and to meet a demand is to answer it

explanation.surface: Someone looked into a lamb's case and gave a considered reply.
explanation.walkthrough: Read in the past tense rhymes with bed; meet means answer, as in meeting a challenge.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamb is an example of red meat, along with beef and mutton.

clue.text: Child with a broad smile causes annoyance

parts.note: CH is a standard abbreviation for child
'with' joins; the article stays
a grin is a broad smile

explanation.surface: A child's cheeky grin irritates the adults around them.
explanation.definitionFit: Chagrin is vexation or annoyance at being humiliated or disappointed.

clue.text: Funny, Colonel drinking mineral

indicators.note: a drinker takes something in, so the officer word holds the other inside

parts.note: Col is the abbreviation for colonel
mica is a shiny silicate mineral that splits into flakes

explanation.surface: An amusing sight: a colonel downing mineral water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mineral' suggests mineral water, but it is a rock mineral.
explanation.definitionFit: Comical means causing laughter, amusing.

clue.text: Composer drowned in Poole Harbour

indicators.note: something drowned in water is submerged, so the letters lie under the surface of the following words

parts.note: the run straddles the end of the town name and the start of the second word

explanation.surface: A composer met his death in the waters of Poole Harbour, on the Dorset coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Lehár was the Hungarian composer of the operetta The Merry Widow.

clue.text: Song lyric by the French female

parts.note: a lay is a short song or lyric poem
la is the French feminine form of the

explanation.surface: The words of a song written by a Frenchwoman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'female' looks like part of the French phrase, but it is the definition: a woman's name, also famous from the Eric Clapton song.
explanation.definitionFit: Layla is a woman's given name, so a female, as crosswords often define first names.

clue.text: What ex-soldier may have worn in mass rally — black fill the bill?

parts.note: a demo is a mass demonstration or protest rally
B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black
to suit is to be just what is needed

explanation.surface: A veteran marching at a big protest, asked whether black clothing would do.
explanation.walkthrough: A demob suit was the civilian suit issued to British servicemen on demobilisation after the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Demobbed soldiers were given a civilian outfit to wear on leaving the forces.

clue.text: Knock over raised object

parts.note: something raised is up
an end is an aim or object, as in means to an end

explanation.surface: Someone topples an item that had been lifted up.
explanation.definitionFit: To upend something is to turn it upside down or tip it over.

clue.text: Play a song written by Chuck Berry

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a comedy by George Bernard Shaw

definitions.text: a song written by Chuck Berry
definitions.meaning: second meaning: his 1964 rock and roll hit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Play a song' reads as an instruction to a DJ; 'Play' is the first definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: The title belongs both to a Shaw comedy of 1897 and to a Chuck Berry single of 1964.

clue.text: Article located involved storytelling

indicators.note: something involved is tangled up, so the following word's letters are rearranged

parts.note: the indefinite article
the seven letters reordered

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece was found to be mixed up in tall tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Anecdotal means based on personal stories rather than hard evidence, an adjective like storytelling used attributively.

clue.text: Hot and exceptionally dry round health spa

indicators.note: exceptionally means out of the ordinary, so the next word's letters leave their usual order

parts.note: H is the tap abbreviation for hot
the three letters reordered
a round shape looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A health resort described as very hot and arid all around.
explanation.walkthrough: A hydro is a British term for a hotel or resort offering water treatments.
explanation.definitionFit: A hydro is a hydropathic establishment, a spa for therapeutic baths.
